newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FOCUS-South Africans in no rush to invest offshore.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-South Africans in no rush to invest offshore.

text.p: South African individuals have been in no great rush to invest in foreign markets since being given a green light on July 1 to take funds overseas for the first time in 30 years.
The central Reserve Bank said on Friday that private individuals invested 144 million rands offshore or in foreign exchange bank accounts during July.

That is only a fraction of the three to five billion rand ($1.1 billion) that Reserve Bank officials have predicted could leave the country over a period of months following the landmark easing of exchange controls.

However, while the level outflows from individuals may have been modest, the country's official reserves of gold and foreign exchange appear to have been depleted by central bank intervention in support of the rand.

The Bank said reserves stood at 22.8 billion rand in July from June's 22.13 billion rand. But this was after an increase in the use of foreign credit lines to 3.2 billion rand from 1.8 billion rand at end-June and the benefit of $250 million from the government's recent Yankee bond issue.
The total figure will have been reduced following the fall in the gold price, although foreign buying of stocks and bonds was a positive factor in the month.
The currency has been under pressure in recent weeks, hit by fears about the impact of a plunge in gold prices -- which hit a 12-year low earlier this month -- and a strong U.S. dollar.
On Friday it broke below 4.63 to the dollar for the first time in 6-1/2 months.

Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals said on Thursday that the authorities had been particularly active in supporting the rand in the first half of July following the introduction of the new exchange control regime and the decline in the gold price.
Private South Africans are now allowed to invest up to 200,000 rand offshore or in foreign exchange accounts with local banks.
